sentences.en: This morning I was going to take the train to Shanghai, but I got up late.
Mom glanced at the time and shouted: "Hurry up, there's no time left!"
I quickly threw on my clothes, grabbed my bag, and ran straight outside.

t: to go out; to leave home
sentences.en: As I left, I saw that the bus had already driven off.
I was anxious, so I had no choice but to take a taxi to the train station.

t: there's still time; not too late
sentences.en: The taxi driver said: "Don't worry, we still have time."
By the time I got to the train station, the train was leaving in five minutes.
I made it onto the train, and only once I sat down did the panic settle.

vocab: there's still time; not too late

quiz.q: Why was the narrator in such a rush that morning?
a: Had to catch a train to Shanghai and got up late
Had to go to a job interview

quiz.q: What did the taxi driver say?
How did the narrator feel after finally getting on the train?

grammar.e: 快 + 一点 (often shortened to 快点) is a common way to urge someone to move faster — usually said as a short, urgent command.
grammar.x: 快一点，来不及了！— Hurry up, there's no time!

grammar.p: 来不及 vs. 来得及
grammar.e: 来不及 means there isn't enough time left to do something; 来得及 means the opposite — there's still time. Both are often used with 了 or 还.
grammar.x: 别着急，我们还来得及。— Don't worry, we still have time.

grammar.p: 着…就… (do one thing, then right away another)
grammar.e: 着 marks an action still in progress; adding 就 + another verb shows what happens immediately after, often in a hurry.
grammar.x: 我拿着包就往外面跑。— I grabbed my bag and ran straight outside.
